Good morning, Yamuna. It's Sunday the eighth of November, and this morning's art news has a pleasingly local start before it wanders off to Lyon, London and Washington.

Let's begin in Grenoble, where the Musée de Grenoble has a busy few days. This afternoon at half past two there is a guided tour of the Anne Truitt exhibition, "Libérer la couleur", devoted to the American artist. If you fancy a Sunday walk in the city, it's a timely chance to see the show with someone talking you through it. Yesterday afternoon the museum also offered a guided tour of the François Morellet display, "Sous la géométrie, la facétie", which means "under the geometry, the mischief". That tour has now passed, but the title alone tells you what to expect: Morellet's geometric abstraction was always playful, and the display is a good way into his work. Then, from next Saturday, the fourteenth of November, the museum opens an exhibition on Edmund Kesting, presented as painter, photographer and advertising artist. I like the angle. It sets fine art beside commercial image-making, and asks what happens when one artist moves between the two.

Two smaller local stories, both a little thin on detail. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on an exhibition in Saint-Martin-d'Hères that traces forty years of painting and spiritual searching. The article doesn't give dates, so it may be worth a quick check before you set out. And in Cessieu, a village not far away, there is a digital treasure hunt in search of the village's secret paintings. Details are brief, but it sounds like a charming way to spend an afternoon looking at walls.

Now to Lyon, and to photography. Le Petit Bulletin reports that since the second of November there have been two exhibitions of Blaise Adilon's photographs, one at Le Bleu du Ciel and one at the maison Georges Adilon, along with a new monograph. The work asks how one might provoke the real into producing another image, which is a lovely, slightly mysterious way of describing what a photograph does. Further afield, in Saint-Étienne, "La Ville travaille" runs until the third of March next year. It is two complementary photography exhibitions, one showing the results of artists' residencies and the other a photographic collection about how a working city has changed. Both ask how one can photograph a city at work.

That brings me to images that carry history, which I suspect is where your heart lies. The Guardian points to "Remember Me", which opened on the seventh of November at the National Gallery of Art in Washington and runs until the fourteenth of March 2027. It brings together seventy works showing how African Americans used portrait photography to depict themselves and their communities, with themes of identity, resilience and belonging. In Hyperallergic, Catherine Ostler follows the two girls in Renoir's "Pink and Blue", whose comfortable life in an elite, artistic French family was overturned by the Holocaust. It's a painting that sounds sweet and turns out to be a story about history, and it might make a good starting point for a class on how a picture can hide a whole biography. Also from The Guardian, there is a new exhibition at the V&A in South Kensington, running from the seventh of November to the ninth of May. It traces one city's layered history, from Ottoman court tulips and silks all the way back to Emperor Constantine's palace.

A small gem from the same paper, and I couldn't leave it out. The Guardian profiles a phone photograph by Priya Ojha of the ghat on the sacred Yamuna in New Delhi. She waited in dense fog from around five in the morning, and when the sun finally broke through, the scene turned painterly. She calls it her reward for waiting in the cold. I thought you'd enjoy seeing your own name on a river, and a story about patience paying off.

On the question of language and art, Revue Esprit has published an essay asking whether contemporary art has lost its poetry. Only the question itself is available to us, but it's a good one, and it touches directly on where painting meets the written word. You may want to carry it around for a few days and see which artists you would call as witnesses for the defence.

Finally, a few items from the wider art world. The National Gallery in London has released a video about its NG Citizens project, in which fifty people chosen by civic lottery met in a citizens' assembly to consider how the Gallery can bring people and paintings closer together. It is a thoughtful look at what a national collection is actually for. Hyperallergic's newsletter, "Please Don't Sit on the Flowers", gives a quick round of news: a long-lost Georgia O'Keeffe landscape heading to auction, a Brancusi misplaced at MoMA, an interview with Doris Salcedo, and the question of whether documenta is worth seeing. And if you're tempted by a weekend trip, Beaux Arts Magazine has a guide to five exhibitions across Lorraine and Alsace. It includes the luxuriant paintings of Séraphine Louis in Metz and the glass vases of Émile Gallé in Nancy, which neatly joins painting and craft. The extract doesn't give dates, so that would need checking.

That's the lot for today, Yamuna. Enjoy the Truitt, if you go, and may all your waiting in the cold be rewarded with light.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Sunday the eighth of November, and this weekend's art news begins close to home in Grenoble, then travels out to Lyon, a few other French cities, and a handful of stories from London, Washington and beyond.

Let me start at the Musée de Grenoble, where there's something on today. At half past two this afternoon, there's a guided tour of the exhibition devoted to Anne Truitt, called "Libérer la couleur", or freeing colour. If you haven't yet seen the show, a Sunday tour is a pleasant way to do it, with someone guiding your eye through the work rather than leaving you to wander. The title promises an exhibition about colour as something that can stand on its own, and a guide is often most useful with that kind of work, because it asks you to slow down and look for longer than usual.

Yesterday afternoon, the museum also held a guided tour of its François Morellet display, which carries the lovely title "Sous la géométrie, la facétie", or "Under the geometry, the mischief". That tour has already taken place, but the title is worth holding on to. Morellet is known for playful geometric abstraction, and I like the idea that behind the strict grid there's a sense of humour waiting to be noticed. It's a nice thing to bring to your seconde students, actually, because it suggests that even the most rule-bound art can be a joke told with a straight face. If you'd like to see it, I'd check with the museum on how long the display continues.

Looking ahead, from the fourteenth of November the Musée de Grenoble opens an exhibition on Edmund Kesting, presented as painter, photographer and advertising artist. I find that combination rather appealing. We tend to separate fine art from commercial image-making, as though one were noble and the other merely useful, and an exhibition that puts both in the same room invites us to ask where the real boundary lies. It's a fresh angle for a visit, and a good reason to go to the museum twice this month, once for Truitt and once for Kesting.

A little further out, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on an exhibition in Saint-Martin-d'Hères that retraces forty years of painting and spiritual searching. The article, at least in the extract I have, is thin on dates and practical details, so I can't tell you when it opens or closes. But the theme is a personal and contemplative one: a lifetime of work shaped by the question of what lies beyond the visible. If it appeals, a quick call to the commune's cultural service should give you the details. It's the kind of local show that often turns out to be more moving than its modest billing suggests.

There's also a small, playful story from the village of Cessieu, where a digital treasure hunt invites visitors to look for the village's secret paintings. The report in mesinfos is very brief, so I know little more than that. But I like the idea of art hidden in plain sight, turning a village walk into a game. If you're ever looking for an outing that costs nothing and might amuse a younger visitor, this might be one to keep in mind.

Now to Lyon. Since the second of November, there have been two exhibitions of the photographer Blaise Adilon, one at Le Bleu du Ciel and one at the maison Georges Adilon, together with a new monograph. Le Petit Bulletin Grenoble describes the work as asking how to provoke the real into producing another image. That's a wonderfully literary way of putting it, I think. It suggests a photographer who doesn't simply record the world but coaxes it into revealing something it wouldn't otherwise show, a bit like a novelist who waits for a scene to say what it truly means. The title of the piece, "les images au-delà du visible", images beyond the visible, points the same way. It would make a good Saturday in Lyon, with two venues and a book to take home.

Staying with photography, but heading to Saint-Étienne: until the third of March, twenty twenty-seven, two complementary exhibitions there look at how a working city has changed. One shows the results of photographic residencies, and the other presents a photo collection, and together they ask how a city at work can be photographed. It's called "La Ville travaille", the city works. There's something quietly historical in that, because industrial towns tell their story through faces, factories and streets, and photographs hold on to that more honestly than many textbooks do. With a long run until March, it's an easy one to fit into a winter weekend.

For a longer trip, Beaux Arts Magazine has put together a guide to five exhibitions across Lorraine and Alsace. Among them are the luxuriant paintings of Séraphine Louis in Metz and the glass vases of Émile Gallé in Nancy. I should say the extract doesn't give dates, so you would need to check before travelling. But I enjoy the pairing: a painter whose lush canvases seem to overflow with growth, and a glass-maker who turned plants and light into objects. It's a trip that links painting and craft, which is a good way to think about how art and everyday beauty overlap.

Let me turn now to stories where paintings and photographs carry history, which I suspect will interest you most.

Hyperallergic has a piece by Catherine Ostler about Renoir's painting "Pink and Blue". She follows the two girls in the picture, whose privileged lives in an elite, artistic French family were overturned by the Holocaust. What I like about this approach is that it starts with a picture many people know as simply charming, two children in soft, sweet colours, and then asks what happened to them afterwards. It is history told through a painting and a family, and it's the kind of piece that changes how you see an image you thought you already understood. If you ever teach a lesson on how a portrait can hide a story, this might be a beautiful way into it, because the delicacy of the painting and the weight of what followed sit so uncomfortably side by side.

The Guardian, meanwhile, shows a selection of early Black portrait photography from an exhibition called "Remember Me", which opened on the seventh of November at the National Gallery of Art in Washington and runs until the fourteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven. It brings together seventy works showing how African Americans used portrait photography to depict themselves and their communities. The themes the Guardian highlights are identity, resilience and community. I find it moving to think of a portrait as an act of self-definition, a person deciding how they wish to be seen, at a time when others were all too ready to decide for them. It pairs well, in a way, with the Renoir story: two different ways in which a picture holds a life and a history.

In London, the Guardian's week in art mentions an exhibition at the V&A in South Kensington, running from the seventh of November to the ninth of May. It traces a story from Ottoman court tulips and silks back to the palace of the Emperor Constantine. So it's the layered history of a single city, told through objects, textiles and flowers, moving back through the centuries. For a reader who likes learning history through culture rather than through dates and treaties, that sounds like a good one, and with a run until May, there's plenty of time should you find yourself in London.

Another small Guardian piece is one I couldn't leave out. It profiles Priya Ojha's best phone picture, a photograph of the ghat on the sacred Yamuna in New Delhi. Yes, the river that shares your name. She waited in dense fog from around five in the morning, and when the sun finally broke through, the scene turned painterly. In her words, her reward for waiting in the cold was a painting-like view. I like it as a small story about patience, and about the way light can turn an ordinary morning into something a painter might have chosen. It also makes a nice point for students: that looking carefully, and waiting, is part of making any image, whether on a phone or on canvas.

Then there are a few pieces about how we think about art itself.

Revue Esprit has an essay titled "L'art contemporain a-t-il perdu sa poésie ?", asking whether contemporary art has lost its poetry. All I have is the question, not the argument that follows, but the question is a good one, and it speaks directly to your interests, to that border between visual art and written language. It makes me wonder what we mean by poetry in a gallery. Is it an image that suggests more than it says, or a rhythm, or a kind of silence? You could easily put that question to a première class, asking them to choose a painting and a poem that they feel belong together, and to say why.

On a different note, the National Gallery in London has released a video about a project called NG Citizens. Fifty people, chosen by civic lottery, met in a citizens' assembly to consider how the Gallery can bring people and paintings together. The video asks what the National Gallery should mean to the people it belongs to. It's a thoughtful question for any national collection, and perhaps for local museums too. Who is a museum for, and who gets to decide what it should be? It's pleasant to see an institution put that question to ordinary people rather than to experts alone.

And finally, if you'd like a quick round of art-world news, Hyperallergic's newsletter, "Please Don't Sit on the Flowers", gathers several stories. A long-lost Georgia O'Keeffe landscape is heading to auction, a Brancusi has been misplaced at MoMA, there's an interview with the artist Doris Salcedo, and the newsletter asks whether documenta is worth seeing. It's a light but varied read, and the misplaced Brancusi in particular sounds like the start of a gentle mystery, though I can't tell you how it ends.

So, to sum up the week for you in Grenoble: Anne Truitt this afternoon, Kesting opening on the fourteenth, and the Morellet display, whose mischief you may still catch. Beyond that, there's a photographer in Lyon to look for, a working city in Saint-Étienne, and a few pictures, from Renoir's two girls to a foggy morning on the Yamuna, that remind us how much a single image can hold.

Enjoy the rest of your Sunday, and I hope there's a little colour in it.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Booker-flavoured couple of days in the book pages, with a Scottish prize, a Monet-inspired poem and a few good reading tips tucked in alongside.

Let's start with the Booker shortlist, since most of the conversation is gathered around it. The Guardian has a lovely piece called Narrative Threads, in which this year's finalists, among them Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout, describe where their novels began. The teaser promises a trip to the Scottish islands, a psychological experiment and a chance encounter in a drugstore. It's the sort of article that tells you how a story starts, which is often more revealing than any summary of the plot. Meanwhile, The Irish Times has a critic who has read the whole of the 2026 shortlist and singles out two novels as brilliant on what it feels like to live through the mess of the 2020s. If you're choosing what to read next, that's a useful place to begin. And Prospect Magazine has an essay called The Book That Booker Missed. All I have is the headline, so I can't tell you which book it champions or how the argument runs, but it may be worth a look for the title alone.

The Booker Prizes website is also doing some quiet, bookish work. It has an extract from Max Porter's Lanny, which gives you a direct taste of that novel's voice and language, and should suit your ear for music in prose. There is also a reading guide to Lanny, though the text I have is only the title, so I can't say how far it goes into the narration or style. Then there's a list of eight Booker books inspired by folklore, which connects prize-winning fiction to myth and older storytelling traditions. That might make a nice thread for a class, if you ever want to show how modern novels borrow from much older tales.

Staying with the Booker, but looking backwards, Firstpost has a piece in which a Gen Z reader reviews Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things. It's a fresh and rather sharp take on a novel with one of the most distinctive narrative voices and some of the most lyrical prose among the prizewinners. I'd be curious to know whether it sounds like what your seconde and première students would say.

Now to some good news from Scotland. Douglas Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain, has won the Scottish Book of the Year and, according to ScottishNews, made history in doing so. The Scotsman, which seems to be reporting a Scottish Book of the Year win too, calls the winning novel a masterpiece by one of the finest Scottish novelists writing today. I can't say from what I have that these are definitely the same book, but it's a pleasing result either way for a writer so admired for his Glasgow setting and for characters you carry around long after the last page.

On to poetry, and a link to painting, which I know you like. The Guardian has a roundup of recent poetry, and one collection stands out: Jessica Mookherjee's The Universe Is an Animal. It mixes the language of science with family histories of partition and displacement, which sounds like a striking combination. And one poem in it reworks Monet's waterlilies into something darker. It's a small, intriguing example of a painting being read against the grain, and I think it would sit beautifully beside the familiar, serene picture.

For lovers of thrillers and unusual forms, there are three pieces. The Hindu reviews All Them Dogs by Djamel White, which it describes as Irish gangster noir meeting a forbidden love story. That is a promising mix of menace and tenderness, and noir tends to live or die by its characters. The New Yorker, for its part, reviews the latest issue of Chris Ware's Acme Novelty Library. It calls it a thoroughly modern reading experience, packaged in a keepsake box. Ware is a master of formal invention, so it's a reminder that a book can be an object as well as a text. And in The Paris Review, the musician MJ Lenderman writes about discovering Harry Crews by word of mouth, starting with A Feast of Snakes. He calls him, in the headline's words, a fairly wild guy. The teaser is short, but it looks like a personal essay about a raw, unforgettable writer, and the best kind of recommendation: one reader pressing a book into another's hands.

Finally, two pieces from Literary Hub. In the daily edition for the sixth of November, Katherine Kelaidis writes about Sergey Davydov. She argues that stories of ordinary life matter most in times of political upheaval, because it is love, rather than conflict, that drives his inner world. It's a thoughtful essay about perspective in fiction, and about why the small and domestic may be the more truthful lens on turbulent times. The weekly roundup for the second to the sixth of November also includes a piece on how J.R.R. Tolkien's Catholic faith shaped his writing, and Ed Simon on Guy Fawkes and the afterlife of V for Vendetta. The text I have is cut off, so I can only give you those two highlights, but both touch on how stories and history keep feeding each other.

So there's plenty to dip into over a coffee, and I hope one of these ends up on your bedside table.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Booker-flavoured Sunday in the reading world, with a Scottish prize, a poem that borrows from Monet, and a few essays about why we read.

Let me start with the Booker, since much of the conversation is still circling it. The Guardian has a lovely idea for a piece, called "How to write a Booker-shortlisted novel". This year's finalists, among them Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout, each describe where their book began. The teaser promises a trip to the Scottish islands, a psychological experiment, and a chance encounter in a drugstore. I like that mix, because it shows how a novel can start from something very small: a place, an overheard moment, a question about how people behave. If you ever want to show your première students that a book doesn't arrive fully formed, this might be a gentle way in. Hearing novelists talk about origins can make the finished work feel less intimidating and more human.

Alongside it, The Irish Times has a critic who says they have read the whole 2026 shortlist, and who singles out two novels as brilliant on what it is like to live through the mess of the 2020s. The piece doesn't tell me in my notes which two, so I can't name them, but it is a proper literary assessment of the books themselves rather than prize gossip, which makes it a useful guide if you're deciding what to put on your own list. It's interesting to see a critic asking which novels capture the disorder of right now, because that's a question about whether fiction can catch the texture of a moment while we're still inside it. Historical novels often do the reverse, looking back, so it's worth noticing when a writer attempts the present tense of an era.

There's also a note of dissent. Prospect Magazine has an essay called "The book that Booker missed". I only have the headline, so I can't tell you which book it champions or what the argument is. But the title alone is a reminder that every prize list is also a list of absences, and the essay might make good conversation if you track it down.

The Booker Prizes site itself is generous this week with material that goes straight to the writing. There's an extract from Max Porter's Lanny, which gives you a direct taste of the novel's voice and language. Since you love prose that's beautiful as sound as well as sense, this is the sort of passage worth reading aloud to yourself, and perhaps to a class, to hear how it moves. The same site also offers a reading guide to Lanny. I only have the title of that guide, so I can't say how far it goes into narration or style, but a guide from the prize itself is likely to be a tidy starting point if you were thinking of teaching the book or discussing it with colleagues.

The third Booker Prizes piece is a list of eight prize-winning novels inspired by folklore. That connects fiction to myth and older storytelling traditions, and I think it fits the way you like novels to carry history and culture along with them. A list like this is a quiet reminder that many modern narrators are, in one way or another, inheriting the voice of the village storyteller, and it could be a nice thread to pull for a class who think of folk tales as something only for children.

Staying with the Booker, but looking back rather than forward, Firstpost has a piece in a series called "A Gen Z Reviews the Classics". This time the reader revisits Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things, a Booker winner, and finds it has a very sharp edge. What appeals to me here is the fresh pair of eyes. You know better than most how it feels when a younger reader comes to a celebrated book without the weight of its reputation, and sometimes sees its voice and its lyrical prose more clearly than those of us who learned to revere it first. Roy's narration is so musical and so full of memorable characters that it's easy to imagine a student's honest reaction being more useful than a polished critical one. It might be worth reading as a sample of how a younger reader talks about style.

From the Booker to a Scottish prize. Douglas Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain, has won Scottish Book of the Year, and ScottishNews.com says he has made history with the award. I don't have the details of what exactly the history is, so I won't guess, but it is a heartening result for a novelist whose Glasgow setting and strong characters so many readers admire. The Scotsman also reports on a Scottish Book of the Year win, calling the winning work a masterpiece by one of the finest Scottish novelists writing today. The text I have doesn't name the author or the book, so I can't be certain it is the same win, although the timing suggests it very well might be. Either way, it is a good week for Scottish fiction, and it pairs neatly with Stuart's name appearing on the Booker shortlist as well.

Now to something quieter, and one of the pieces I think you'll enjoy most. The Guardian has a review roundup of recent poetry, and it includes Jessica Mookherjee's collection The Universe Is an Animal. The collection mixes the language of science with family histories of partition and displacement, which is a striking pairing: the vocabulary of the cosmos set beside the stories of people who were forced to leave their homes. And, for someone who loves the links between painting and writing, there's one poem in the collection that reworks Monet's waterlilies into something darker. I don't have the poem itself, so I can't tell you how, but the idea is irresistible. Those paintings are so often treated as a pure image of calm, and to see a poet turn them towards something shadowed is exactly the sort of dialogue between canvas and page that makes ekphrasis such a rewarding form. If you're ever looking for a way to bring a painting into a poetry lesson, a poem that complicates a familiar image might be more useful than one that simply admires it.

Let me turn now to books that stretch the form, or that live on the rough edges of it. The New Yorker reviews the latest issue of Chris Ware's Acme Novelty Library, which the piece describes as a thoroughly modern reading experience, packaged in a keepsake box. The headline calls it a fractal pandemic chronicle. Ware is a cartoonist and a formal inventor, and his work asks you to read in several directions at once, with pages that behave more like architecture than like a plain run of sentences. I don't have the details of the contents, but a book that arrives in a box, to be handled and explored, seems like an argument for the physical object in an age of screens. If you're interested in how stories can be told by design as well as by words, it may be worth the read, even if only the review.

If you want a thriller, The Hindu has a review of All Them Dogs by Djamel White, which the headline describes as Irish gangster noir meets forbidden love. I only have that headline to go on, so I can't speak to the plot or the style. But the combination is a good one: noir has always been about voice and atmosphere, and a love story that isn't allowed to happen gives it a human centre. It sounds like a book for a long evening by the stove rather than a quick read.

And for something rawer, The Paris Review has musician MJ Lenderman writing about Harry Crews. He discovered Crews by word of mouth, beginning with a novel called A Feast of Snakes, and the essay is titled, bluntly, "This Fucked-Up Guy". Forgive the language, it is the headline. The teaser is short, but the piece is a personal essay about a writer who evidently left a mark, and I like that it begins the way so many reading lives begin, with someone simply telling you that you have to read this. It's also a good example of a reader who isn't a critic describing what a book did to them, which might be a useful model for students writing about their own responses.

Finally, two pieces from Literary Hub that are more about the habit of reading than about any one book. In the Lit Hub Daily for the sixth of November, Katherine Kelaidis writes about Sergey Davydov and argues that stories of ordinary life matter most during political upheaval, because it is love rather than conflict that drives his inner world. I find that a thoughtful idea. It suggests that in turbulent times the novel's job isn't necessarily to mirror the turbulence, but to keep alive the smaller, steadier things that people actually live by. It echoes, in a way, that Irish Times question about novels of the 2020s, though from the opposite direction.

The Lit Hub Weekly, covering the second to the sixth of November, is a roundup, and my text of it is cut short. The highlights I can see are a piece on how J.R.R. Tolkien's Catholic faith shaped his writing, and an essay by Ed Simon on Guy Fawkes and the afterlife of V for Vendetta. The Tolkien piece could be of interest for thinking about how belief seeps into invented worlds, and the Guy Fawkes essay is a good one for this week, with Bonfire Night having just passed, since it follows how a historical figure becomes a mask, then a symbol, then a story told again and again. That's history learned through fiction, which I know is close to your heart.

So there is the shape of the weekend: the Booker conversation continuing, a Scottish win to celebrate, a Monet turned dark in a poem, and a handful of writers explaining why they read.

I hope you find a good page to settle into with your coffee this morning.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Sunday the eighth of November, and the valley and Grenoble have a quiet mix of art, music and local stories on offer, some of it today and some a little further ahead.

Let me start with today, because two things are worth knowing about. It is the last day of Hervé Frumy's exhibition "Les Yeux Ouverts" at Le Belvédère, the cultural centre Jeannine Creissels in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage. It opened on the twenty-sixth of September, so if a Sunday outing appeals, this is your final chance. I don't have opening hours, so a quick check before setting off would be wise. Also today, from ten in the morning until six in the evening, the salle des fêtes in Saint-Vincent-de-Mercuze hosts an autumn market of local producers. It's a good opportunity for regional produce, and a pleasant way to spend a November morning in the Grésivaudan.

Now, a thread that runs through the week: photography. Since yesterday, and until the twenty-ninth of November, Grenoble is holding a month-long photography programme, Le mois de la photo, and the listing says it's free. The catch is that it names no venues and no photographers, so think of it as a lead to follow up rather than a firm plan. A more concrete date comes this Tuesday, the tenth of November, at seven in the evening, at Espace Aragon in Villard-Bonnot. There's an evening devoted to Vivian Maier, under the title "Tout entière", which roughly means "in her entirety". Given how much her pictures feel like stories caught mid-sentence, it seems a natural fit for someone who likes to put images and narrative side by side.

Yesterday saw two small gatherings that you may have missed, and they're worth mentioning for the spirit of them. At the village hall in Saint-Jean-le-Vieux, there was an evening of Belledonne-themed storytelling and gatherings, running from half past six until ten. And in the morning, at the library in La Combe-de-Lancey, three artists met visitors between ten and one. The listing doesn't say what kind of art they make. Both have passed now, but they show that the winter evenings in Belledonne are filling up with this sort of thing, so keep an ear out for the next one.

On to the stage and the concert hall. Le Dauphiné Libéré has a piece about a guided visit behind the scenes of the Grand Théâtre de Grenoble. The date isn't given in the text, but it promises a rare look at how a stage actually works, the machinery behind the magic. The same paper reports that readers can meet the singer Raphaël before his concert at the MC2 in Grenoble, though again the date isn't stated, so the MC2 itself would be the place to confirm timing. And a Grenoble by Night feature in the Dauphiné looks at La Belle Électrique, describing it as much more than a concert hall, a place to let go and feel the music. Only the standfirst was available, so I can't say how deep the article goes.

Further ahead, on the third of December at six in the evening, the Théâtre Hexagone in Meylan presents "Hypertemps". It's Clément Edouard's one-hour sound installation and performance, exploring time, rhythm and listening, and there are three further dates after the first. It sounds like something for a person who listens closely to the music of language as well as of sound. And looking right across to next year, the Hexagone is also behind the thirteenth edition of the EXPERIMENTA biennial, in 2027. There are no dates yet, but it's promising eighty proposals of exhibitions, shows and performances, drawn from twenty-three partners across the territory.

At the MC2 in Grenoble, there is also a programme of free cultural activities for people with disabilities running throughout November. It's a welcome, inclusive initiative, and a good thing to see in a major venue.

Finally, a few items on community and heritage. In Chambéry, Le Dauphiné Libéré tells of volunteers who are restoring old trains and putting them back on the rails. It's a warm story about people doing something patient and worthwhile, with a touch of nostalgia about it. In the Grésivaudan, the Festival des solidarités opens on the twelfth of November. I only have the headline, so the programme and venues are unknown, but it is a community event in the valley and may be worth watching for details this week. And Échosciences Grenoble has announced the thirteenth Rencontres Montagnes & Sciences, a meeting on mountains and science. Again there's only a title, with no dates or venues confirmed, though it could appeal given where you live, under Belledonne.

So, a market, a final exhibition, a photographer's evening on Tuesday and plenty of stages to look forward to; I hope your Sunday has a little of each.
around.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Sunday the eighth of November, and the last couple of days have left a pleasant scatter of things around you, from a final-day exhibition to a market on your doorstep to a few leads worth keeping in your diary.

Let me begin with today, since two things are on the clock. First, at Le Belvédère, the Centre Culturel Jeannine Creissels in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage, today is the last day of Hervé Frumy's exhibition, Les Yeux Ouverts. It opened on the twenty-sixth of September, so it has had a good run, but this is your final chance. The listing doesn't tell us what the work looks like or what the opening hours are today, so if you fancy a Sunday outing, a quick check before you set off would be wise. It's the kind of local show that suits a quiet, unhurried afternoon, the sort where you stand in front of a picture for a while and let it tell you what it wants to.

Second, today from ten in the morning until six in the evening, there is an autumn producers' market at the salle des fêtes in Saint-Vincent-de-Mercuze, in the Grésivaudan. It's a chance to buy regional produce close to home, and I know that's a pleasure of yours. November is a good moment for it, with the season turning towards soups, roasts and things you want to bring home in a basket. If you combine the two, a morning at the market and an afternoon with the Frumy exhibition, you'd have a proper valley Sunday, though I'd check the travel between the two before promising yourself both.

Now, a theme that I think will appeal to you particularly: photography, and the way images and stories meet. On Tuesday the tenth of November, at seven in the evening, Espace Aragon in Villard-Bonnot hosts an evening devoted to the photographer Vivian Maier. It's part of a series with the lovely format of one evening, one artist, and this one is titled Tout entière. The listing gives us little beyond that, but Maier is exactly the sort of artist who sits at the crossroads of image and narrative, where a single photograph can feel like the first line of a novel. If you teach your students to read a scene closely, to notice what is placed where and what is left out, there is something in an evening like this that would feed straight back into the classroom. It's a weekday evening, so it would suit after school, and Villard-Bonnot is comfortably in the valley.

Alongside that, Grenoble is hosting Le mois de la photo, a month-long photography programme running from the seventh to the twenty-ninth of November. It is listed as free, which is always welcome. I should be honest that the listing gives no venues and no names of featured photographers, so I'd treat it as a lead to follow up rather than a plan. But with three weeks of it still ahead of us, you have time to look into what's on, and it sits very naturally beside the Maier evening. You might think of the two together as a small photographic thread running through your November.

Let me turn now to stories and conversations, because two small gatherings took place yesterday that are worth knowing about, even though they have passed. On Saturday the seventh of November, from half past six until ten in the evening, the village hall at Saint-Jean-le-Vieux hosted an evening of storytelling and gatherings on the theme of Belledonne, the veillées of the title. The word veillée has a wonderful old sound to it, the idea of neighbours gathering in the evening to share tales, and the theme of Belledonne is of course your own mountain range, the one above your house. The listing says it was a good fit for someone who loves narrators and local life, and I think that's right. I mention it partly because evenings like this tend to come round again, and it's worth keeping an eye on the Grésivaudan agenda for similar ones through the winter, when the long dark evenings suit this sort of thing so well.

Also yesterday, between ten in the morning and one in the afternoon, three artists met visitors at the library in La Combe-de-Lancey. The listing doesn't say what kind of art they make, so I can't tell you whether it was painting, drawing or something else entirely. But a morning spent talking with working artists, in a library of all places, is a fine combination, books on the shelves and people explaining how they make things. If the library runs more of these, it would be one to follow, given your interest in the links between painting and writing.

On to performance and music, where there are several things for the weeks ahead. Looking furthest forward but with a firm date: on Thursday the third of December, at six in the evening, the Théâtre Hexagone in Meylan presents Hypertemps, a one-hour sound installation and performance by Clément Edouard. It explores time, rhythm and listening, and there are three further dates beyond that one, though the listing doesn't give them. For a reader who loves music and who pays close attention to form and language, this sounds intriguing. Poetry is, after all, a matter of rhythm and time, of how long a line lingers, and an hour devoted to listening closely seems like a good antidote to a busy December. It's early in the evening too, so it's not a late night.

In the same vein, there's news about the thirteenth edition of the EXPERIMENTA biennial, with its companion PERFORMA, due in 2027 and linked to the Scène nationale Hexagone in Meylan. No dates have been given yet, so this is one for the horizon. What we do know is the scale of it: eighty proposals of exhibitions, shows and performances, from twenty-three partners across the territory. That's a great deal of art spread across the area, and when the dates are announced it could offer a rich season of things to see close to home. I'd keep it in the back of your mind.

For theatre lovers, there's a guided visit behind the scenes of the Grand Théâtre de Grenoble, reported by jds.fr. The date isn't given in the text, so you'd need to look it up, but it promises a rare look at how a stage actually works. If you love theatre and stories, there's something irresistible about seeing the machinery behind the magic, the wings, the flies, the places where the illusion is made. With students studying plays, it might even give you a few vivid images to bring back to a lesson on staging.

Still in Grenoble, and on the musical side, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on an opportunity for readers to meet the singer Raphaël before his concert at the MC2. The date isn't given in the listing, so you'd want to check with the venue for the concert's timing. I mention it knowing that you may not be a devoted follower, but a chance to hear an artist speak before a concert is a nice thing in itself, as it gives the music a little context.

And the same newspaper has a Grenoble by Night feature on La Belle Électrique, which it presents as much more than a concert hall, a place to feel the music and let go. The text we have is only a standfirst, so I can't say how deep the piece goes. But it's a reminder that Grenoble has a lively venue for live music, should you fancy an evening out of a different kind from the usual.

There's also something quietly lovely happening at the MC2 in Grenoble, reported by mesinfos: free cultural activities for people with disabilities, running throughout November. It's a local cultural programme with an inclusive aim, and it's good to see a major venue opening its doors in this way. We don't have the details of the activities themselves, but if you know anyone who might benefit, or colleagues who would want to pass it on, it runs all month, so there's no rush.

Finally, a few items that speak to community and heritage in the wider area. In Chambéry, Le Dauphiné Libéré tells the story of volunteers who are restoring old trains and putting them back on the rails. It's a warm piece, with a clear sense of people doing something worthwhile together. There's something almost novelistic about it, the patience of restoration, people giving their time to something that might otherwise rust quietly away. If you ever want a story with real characters in it, volunteers like these are a good place to start looking.

In the Grésivaudan, the Festival des solidarités opens on Thursday the twelfth of November. All we have is the headline, so the programme and venues are unknown for now, but it is a community event in the valley, and with four days to go, details should surface soon. It's one to watch for, particularly if you like events with a local, neighbourly feel.

And from Échosciences Grenoble comes an announcement of the thirteenth Rencontres Montagnes et Sciences, a meeting on mountains and science. The text is only a title, so I can't give you dates, venues or a programme. But given where you live, with Belledonne right above your head, a meeting about mountains and how we understand them might well be worth a look once the details appear.

So, to gather it up. For today, the Frumy exhibition's last day and the producers' market at Saint-Vincent-de-Mercuze. For this week, the Vivian Maier evening in Villard-Bonnot on Tuesday and the start of the Festival des solidarités on Thursday. For the month, the photography programme in Grenoble and the free activities at the MC2. And for later, Hypertemps in Meylan in early December, and the great EXPERIMENTA biennial next year. A few of these still need a little checking, but there is plenty to choose from.

Enjoy whatever you choose, Yamuna, and may your Sunday have good light and a full basket.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter couple of days for official BFI news, but there's a pleasing run of stage reviews and reading pieces that touch several of your set texts.

Let me begin with the theatre, since three items point at the twenty twenty-seven programme. The Observer reviews Lost Dog's The Last Hamlet, which it describes as mixing Shakespeare with soft toys and a shambolic charm. I can't tell you more about the staging than that, but the combination is intriguing. A Hamlet that plays with toys and a deliberately untidy air might be a good way to ask your première students what is essential to the play. If you take away the grandeur, what remains? The grief, the doubt, the performing within the performance? Even without seeing it, the review could work as a short reading, with students deciding whether charm and shabbiness suit a tragedy or sharpen it.

Staying with the stage, there is a review from Theatre and Tonic of Great Expectations at the Jack Studio Theatre. Dickens is on the twenty twenty-seven list, and the review gives you a way into thinking about how a long, first-person novel is turned into something performed. Pip tells his own story and is rather unreliable about it, so a stage version must decide what to do with that voice. That question might make a lively exercise: how would you show Pip's retrospective shame in a theatre, with no narrator's commentary?

The third is from closer to the programme's heart. The Westmeath Independent reports that the Mount Temple Drama Group, in Westmeath, Ireland, is staging Brian Friel's Dancing at Lughnasa. The item is brief, but it's a small reminder that Friel's play is very much alive in Irish community theatre, performed by local groups as well as professionals. It might make a nice point for students: a play about five sisters in a remote Donegal household, remembered by a narrator, still being taken up by amateur casts today.

Related to all this, there's a short essay from MiscelAna marking four hundred and ten years since Shakespeare's death and asking why he still matters. The text is brief, so I wouldn't lean on it for argument, but as a prompt it suits a seconde or première opening lesson on Twelfth Night or Hamlet. Students could be asked to agree or disagree with the word "immortal", and to bring one example from either play to back up their view.

Now to the novels. The Irish Times reviews Catherine Cliff's debut, Miss Bates: Emma Revisited, which retells Austen's Emma from the viewpoint of Miss Bates, the gossipy and rather overlooked talker of Highbury. The reviewer calls it witty and ambitious. Emma is on your oral themes list, and I think this one is rich for class. Miss Bates is a character the reader is invited to laugh at, and at Box Hill Emma is cruel to her. Giving her the narration turns that on its head. It lends itself to a lovely exercise on narrative perspective: take a scene from Emma, then rewrite it in the voice of someone standing at the edge of it. I'd be cautious, as I've only the review's verdict to go on, but it's a good candidate for you to look at yourself.

On the more critical side, the Financial Times has an essay called Cormac McCarthy: A Legacy Revisited, about how his reputation became a kind of myth. The extract available is thin, so I can't give you its argument, but the framing is interesting for anyone teaching The Road. It raises the question of how much the author's austere, almost legendary image colours the way we read the book. For oral candidates, that could be a useful habit of mind: to read the text itself, and to notice what reputation adds on top of it.

Then Arab News, in its What We Are Reading Today column, turns to George Orwell's enduring argument for protecting life's simple pleasures. Again the text is slight, but it's a gentle counterweight to the Orwell students know best. 1984 is on the oral list, and it's easy to see him only as the writer of warnings. A column about small pleasures, such as the things worth defending, invites a reflective discussion. What is Winston Smith actually being deprived of, and why do simple, sensory moments matter so much in that book?

Two final items I would flag as a little uncertain, since only the titles came through. AnOther Magazine has an Obsessions Index feature with the composer Max Richter. I can't say what he chooses to talk about, but given your love of classical music and your interest in the links between art forms, it might be worth a look for pleasure rather than for teaching. And on Substack, Joanna Williams has an essay called Why Reading Matters. I can't confirm her argument, and it may well lean toward education policy and debate, which you tend to prefer to avoid, so treat it with caution. Still, the title alone is a good seed for a class conversation: ask students to write their own answer in three sentences before they read anyone else's.

If I had to pick one thing to follow up, it would be the Miss Bates retelling alongside the Hamlet review. Together they show two ways of making a classic strange again: change the voice, or change the staging. Both would give your students something to argue about.

That's your corner for today, Yamuna. I hope the weekend brings a little time for a good book and a cup of something warm.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter couple of days for official BFI news, with nothing on reforms or texts, but there's a pleasing run of theatre, a retelling of Austen, and a few essays on why these writers still matter, so let's start on the stage.

Three of today's items are about live theatre, and all three concern set texts for the twenty twenty-seven session. That's handy for you, because a staging is often the quickest way into a play for a class that finds the page forbidding.

The most unusual is a review in The Observer of a production called The Last Hamlet, from a company called Lost Dog. The reviewer describes a mix of Shakespeare, soft toys and what they call shambolic charm. I can't tell you more than that from what's been supplied, so I won't pretend to know how the soft toys are used, or whether they stand in for characters, for the court, or for something else entirely. But the description alone suggests a way into the play. Hamlet is a text that students often approach with a great deal of reverence, and a production that is playful and a little chaotic invites them to ask what happens to the play when you take away the solemnity. Does it still work? What survives? You could ask a première class to imagine their own unlikely staging choices and defend them with a line from the text. It's a good exercise in reading closely while pretending to be silly, and it tends to produce better annotation than a straight request for analysis.

The second is a review from the site Theatre and Tonic of Dickens's Great Expectations at the Jack Studio Theatre. Again, the summary I have is brief, so I can only say that it is a review of a stage production of the novel. But that is already useful, because Great Expectations has such a strong narrator, and the question of how you put a narrator on stage is an interesting one for students. Pip tells his own story, looking back, and that retrospective voice is much of what makes the book what it is. A stage version must decide what to do with it: give it to one actor, split it among several, or drop it and let the action speak. If you read the review with a class, you might ask what has to be gained and lost when a first-person memory becomes a scene played in front of us. It also fits well with the dramatic energy that Dickens himself brought to public performance, though I'd leave that for you to judge, since it's your territory more than mine.

The third is a short piece from the Westmeath Independent. The Mount Temple Drama Group in Westmeath, Ireland, is staging Brian Friel's Dancing at Lughnasa. The item is brief, essentially an announcement, and I don't have dates or details of casting. Still, there's something quietly lovely about it. This is a local amateur drama group taking on a play that sits on your syllabus, which is a reminder that Friel's play lives in village halls and community theatres as well as in big houses. For a class, that could prompt a conversation about who a play belongs to. Since you love dance and music, Lughnasa may be one of the programme texts that sits most naturally with your own interests, so even a small production notice is worth keeping in the file for later in the year.

Now to fiction, and one of the more intriguing items. The Irish Times reviews a debut novel by Catherine Cliff called Miss Bates: Emma Revisited. As the title suggests, it retells Austen's Emma from the point of view of Miss Bates, the gossipy, overlooked figure in the original. The reviewer calls it witty and ambitious.

I like this for a few reasons. Emma is on the oral themes list, so it's one of the books students may choose to speak about, and a retelling from a minor character's side is a ready-made lesson in narrative perspective. In Austen, Miss Bates is chiefly seen through other people's eyes, and often through Emma's. What happens when she gets to tell it? What do we notice that we didn't before? Students could try the same experiment themselves: take a short scene from Emma, rewrite a paragraph from the viewpoint of someone standing at the edge of it, and then discuss how the choice of narrator changes what the reader sees and judges. It's a wonderful way to teach free indirect discourse by contrast, because students feel the difference as soon as the voice changes. And for you, with your fondness for memorable narrators, there's something appealing in the idea of a character who is usually talked over finally being given the floor. I haven't read the book and the review summary doesn't tell me how it handles that, so I'd treat it as a promising lead rather than a recommendation. A passage or two, if the publisher or newspaper offers an extract, would be worth looking at before you decide whether it belongs in front of a class.

On the subject of critical frames, the Financial Times has an essay titled Cormac McCarthy: A Legacy Revisited, on the making of a myth. What I've been given of the text is thin, so I can only say it's about how McCarthy's reputation has been built up into something larger than the books. That's relevant because The Road is on the oral themes list. When students speak about a novel that already has a mythic aura, there's a risk that they repeat the received wisdom: it's bleak, it's profound, it's about fathers and sons. An essay that asks how a writer's reputation was constructed could encourage a more sceptical, independent reading. You might use the idea, even without the essay in hand, by asking: how much of what we think we know about this book comes from the book itself, and how much from the aura around its author? It's a good question for terminale, and it applies to nearly every author on the list. Given the paywall that the Financial Times sometimes puts up, you may not be able to read the whole thing, so I'd take the title as a prompt rather than rely on the content.

The remaining items are shorter reflections on why writers and reading matter, and they are all rather slight in what I have, so I'll take them quickly and honestly.

First, a short essay from a site called MiscelAna marking four hundred and ten years since Shakespeare's death and asking why he remains immortal. The text is brief. It's the kind of piece that could suit a seconde or première class as a warm-up before starting Twelfth Night or Hamlet, both on the twenty twenty-seven session. You could use it as a provocation rather than an authority. Ask students whether they agree that Shakespeare is immortal, what evidence they'd offer, and whether they think it's true or simply repeated. Then let them test the claim against the first act of whichever play you're about to open. A short, slightly sweeping essay is often better as something to argue with than something to agree with, and that may be its best use here.

Second, an Arab News reading column titled What We Are Reading Today, this time about George Orwell's enduring argument for protecting life's simple pleasures. The text is thin, and I can't say which of Orwell's writings it draws on. But Orwell is on the oral themes list through 1984, and the idea of defending small, ordinary pleasures sits interestingly beside that novel's world, where private feeling and everyday comforts are under threat. I'd be careful not to claim a direct link that the column may not make. Still, as a prompt for reflection, it's rich. You could ask a class why a writer so concerned with power and surveillance would also care about something as modest as a good cup of tea, a garden or a fire in the grate. Is that a contradiction, or the very point? It's a gentle, humane way into a text that students sometimes see only as a warning, and it might appeal to you as someone who values the texture of daily life, markets and all.

Third, there's a Substack essay by Joanna Williams titled Why Reading Matters. All I have is the title, so I can't tell you what the argument is. The subject is close to your heart, but I'd flag that Substack writing on education can lean towards the polemical, and I know that isn't your preference. I'd suggest skipping it unless you happen to be in the mood, and certainly not building anything on it until you've seen what it actually says.

Finally, a small musical aside, since you enjoy classical music. AnOther Magazine has an item in its Obsessions Index series featuring the composer Max Richter. Only the title has come through, so I can't say what he is obsessed with, or whether it touches on literature at all. I mention it because he's a composer whose work many people find hauntingly beautiful, and because the format, a person listing what they love and why, is a nice model for a class activity. Students could write their own short obsessions index about a book, a painting or a piece of music, giving a sentence of reason for each. It's a quiet way of practising personal response, which is exactly what the oral rewards. If you do find the full piece, it might make a pleasant five minutes with a coffee, whatever its relevance to the syllabus.

To pull the threads together, if you want one idea from today to take into class, I'd make it this: the same story changes shape depending on who tells it and who stages it. Hamlet with soft toys, Pip on a small stage, Emma through Miss Bates's eyes, McCarthy as myth, and Orwell as a defender of small pleasures all say that a text is not a fixed object but something we keep reinterpreting. That's a good habit of mind for students to bring to the BFI, and it costs very little to practise.

Nothing today changes your planning, but plenty of it is worth keeping in a folder for later in the year, so enjoy your Sunday, and may all your narrators be reliable, or at least entertainingly unreliable.

good.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a rich couple of days for good news, with rescued animals, long journeys home, and a fair few stories about art and words that I think you'll enjoy.

Let me begin with nature, where there is real encouragement. Good News Network reports that donors from around the world have raised millions to buy an estate that a British noble family held for eight hundred years. It is home to curlew, lapwing and mountain bumblebees, and it will now be protected for wildlife conservation. The article I have is cut off, so I can't tell you more about where it is or how the money was gathered. But the outcome is clear: a very old piece of land, and the birds and bees that live on it, now have a future.

Also from Good News Network, there is the Bangka slow loris, a venomous primate that was feared extinct for a century. It survives, thanks to a local wildlife group on Bangka island that rescues animals and returns them to the wild. It is conservation working on the ground, done by people who live alongside the creatures they protect.

And from the laboratory, The Optimist Daily carries a Stanford podcast about two coral fragments that accidentally touched in a tank. Where they touched, they began absorbing healthy algae from one another. The researchers had not planned this, and it may point to a possible way for bleached coral to recover. The episode covers nine more solutions besides, if you fancy a longer listen.

Now to people, and some lovely stories of perseverance and decency. Karl Bushby, a British former paratrooper, has finished a walk around the world. He set out from Hull in nineteen ninety-eight, and twenty-eight years later he has walked home to his hometown, where his mother was waiting. Good News Network says she was in tears, and I can well imagine it.

Upworthy tells of Eric Schultz, a teenager in Hawaii who spent years in homeless shelters and in his car. He has now graduated from Waianae High School. It is a quiet story of stubbornness and hope, and I thought of your pupils as I read it.

And in southern Brazil, a man named Pedro Moro found a wad of cash in a public square and spent twelve days tracking down its owner. It turned out to be a young construction worker's entire monthly salary, which he had withdrawn to pay for his daughter's needs. Twelve days is a long time to keep knocking on doors for a stranger, and I find that rather moving.

Closer to home, Le Dauphiné Libéré has a warm piece from Chambéry about volunteers who restore old trains and put them back on the rails. It is the sort of heritage work done by people who simply love it, and perhaps one for a weekend outing, if they open to visitors. I don't have those details, so it would be worth checking.

On a similar note, ARTE Regards has a thirty-minute reportage from Rome, available until twenty thirty-one. It visits a seniors' centre in Trastevere that serves more than two thousand retirees, with painting and dance classes, shared meals and plenty of mutual support. It sounds a thoroughly cheering watch, with dance in it too.

There is another community story from Upworthy. A landlord's family evicted an artist who had lived in her home for forty years, in order to claim the murals she had painted by hand. A neighbour with a paint sprayer then offered her a parting gift. I'll leave the detail of what happened for you to discover, but the headline calls it perfect, and the story is about neighbours looking after an artist and the place she made beautiful.

Now to the arts, which I know is your territory. The Guardian has a gallery of early Black portrait photography, from an exhibition called Remember Me at the National Gallery of Art in Washington. It runs from the seventh of November to the fourteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven, and brings together seventy works. They show how African Americans used portraits to depict themselves and their communities, on their own terms. It is a fine example of images that carry history.

Upworthy also has a short piece on a detail that van Gogh hid in his painting Café Terrace at Night, which went unnoticed for a hundred years. I only have the headline and a very brief text, so I can't tell you what the detail is, but it is a nice reminder that a painting you think you know can still hold a secret.

Another small Upworthy story concerns Stevie Nicks, who reportedly misheard a Southern woman's accent, and that single vowel inspired one of her best-known songs. A misheard word becoming art is, I think, rather lovely for anyone who cares about language.

Finally, some news from the world of books. ScottishNews.com reports that Douglas Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain, has won the Scottish Book of the Year and made history with the award. The Scotsman, which appears to be covering the same prize, calls the winning novel a masterpiece by one of the finest Scottish novelists writing today. For a reader who values strong characters and a vivid Glasgow setting, that is a pleasing result.

One last item, which isn't really good news but may interest you as a teacher. An Upworthy parent describes showing Dead Poets Society to their Gen Z children and being floored by how angry the film made them. It is a thoughtful little piece about how a story about teaching lands with a new generation.

That is all for today, Yamuna, and I hope the day treats you as kindly as these stories treated their characters.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. This morning's good news travels from Scottish moorland to a coral tank in California, and from a Hawaiian graduation to a railway workshop not far from you in Chambéry.

Let me begin with nature, where there is some real encouragement. The Good News Network reports that donors from around the world have raised millions to buy an estate that a British noble family held for eight hundred years. It is home to curlew, lapwing and mountain bumblebees, and it will now be protected for wildlife conservation. The article I have is cut off, so I can't tell you the finer details of the sale or exactly where the land lies. But the shape of the story is lovely. An estate that passed down one family line for eight centuries now belongs, in a sense, to a great many strangers who simply wanted the curlews to keep their ground. If you have ever heard a curlew's call, that long, rising, bubbling cry, you will know why people might open their wallets for it.

Also from the Good News Network comes a story from Indonesia. The Bangka slow loris is a venomous primate that people feared had vanished altogether, believed extinct for a hundred years. It has survived, and the credit goes to a local wildlife group on Bangka island that rescues animals and returns them to the wild. What I like here is that it isn't a story about a grand international programme. It is about people on the island itself doing patient, practical work, and the result is an animal that was written off as lost and turns out to be still there.

And from The Optimist Daily, there is a podcast transcript from the sixth of November, built around a small and rather beautiful accident in a Stanford lab. Two coral fragments in a tank happened to touch, and the researchers noticed that through that point of contact, one began absorbing healthy algae from the other. Nobody had planned this. Because bleached coral has lost the algae it depends on, the observation could point to a possible recovery mechanism, a way that damaged coral might heal through contact. It is early, and the researchers themselves hadn't set out to find it, so it is a lead rather than a cure. But many good discoveries begin with someone noticing something unexpected and having the sense to look again. The same episode goes on to cover nine more solutions, if you want a longer listen.

Now to people, and a few stories of perseverance and plain decency.

The Good News Network tells us that Karl Bushby, a British former paratrooper, has finished his walk around the world. He set out from Hull in nineteen ninety-eight, and twenty-eight years later he has come back to his hometown on foot. At the end of it, he was reunited with his mother, who was in tears, and he finally got to hug her. Twenty-eight years is longer than some of your students have been alive, and there is something almost novelistic about the shape of it: a departure, a very long road, and a return to the same front door. I have no more detail than that, but the final image of a son and his mother embracing is a satisfying place for any story to end.

From Hawaii, Upworthy brings us Eric Schultz, a teenager who spent years living in homeless shelters and in his car, and who has now graduated from Waianae High School. The piece is about perseverance, and it will resonate with anyone who teaches. Sitting down to homework and school each day is hard enough with a settled home. To do it through years without one, and to arrive at graduation, is a remarkable achievement, and I hope the day felt as good to him as it sounds.

Then there is a quiet one from southern Brazil, again from the Good News Network. Pedro Moro found a wad of cash in a public plaza. He could simply have pocketed it. Instead he spent twelve days tracking down its owner. The money turned out to be a young construction worker's entire monthly salary, which he had withdrawn to pay for his daughter's needs. Twelve days is a long time to keep knocking on doors and asking questions, and it is a good reminder that honesty is sometimes not a single moment but a sustained effort. The worker got his month's pay back, and his daughter's needs could be met.

Upworthy has another story of community kindness, with a sharper edge. An artist had lived in her home for forty years, and her landlord's family evicted her so that they could claim the murals she had hand-painted there. A neighbour with a paint sprayer then offered her a parting gift. I won't guess at what that gift was, because the piece as I have it doesn't spell it out here, but the headline calls it perfect, and it is a story about art, place, and a neighbour stepping in when it mattered. Forty years of painting a home is a kind of long, slow novel in colour, and it is heartening that someone decided it should have a proper last chapter.

Closer to you, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports from Chambéry on volunteers who restore old trains and put them back on the rails. It is a warm heritage story, about people giving their time to something worthwhile that they can see and touch. I don't have further details such as which trains or where they will run, but if the volunteers hold open days, it might make a pleasant outing from Les Adrets, in the same spirit as your flea markets and local exhibitions. It is good to know that the sound of old rolling stock is being kept alive in Savoie.

For a more contemplative watch, ARTE Concert has put on YouTube an ARTE Regards reportage called Rome : retraités, mais toujours actifs. It visits a seniors' centre in Trastevere that serves more than two thousand retirees, with painting and dance classes, shared meals, and a lot of solidarity. It runs for thirty minutes and, helpfully, is available until twenty thirty-one, so there is no hurry. Given your fondness for dance documentaries and for stories of ordinary lives, it looks like a gentle, uplifting evening's viewing, and it is in French, which suits your lycée life too.

And now to the arts and books, which I suspect are your favourite part of the morning.

The Guardian, in its art and design pages, has a picture feature on early Black portrait photography. It is tied to an exhibition called Remember Me at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, which runs from the seventh of November until the fourteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven. It brings together seventy works showing how African Americans used portrait photography to depict themselves and their communities. The Guardian's headline speaks of identity, resilience and community. It is a strong example of images that carry history: a person choosing how to be seen, in a period when others were all too ready to define them. For a teacher of English literature, it pairs naturally with first-person writing about selfhood, and with the question of who gets to tell a story.

Staying with painting, Upworthy has a short piece on a detail that van Gogh hid in his Café Terrace at Night, one that went unnoticed for a hundred years. The text I have is brief and doesn't say what the detail is, so I won't speculate. But I find the idea irresistible: a painting that people have looked at for a century, and which still held a secret. It is the sort of thing that sends one back to the canvas, and perhaps back to Van Gogh's letters as well, where he wrote so vividly about colour and night.

On to books. Two outlets are reporting on the Scottish Book of the Year. ScottishNews.com says that Douglas Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain, has won the prize and made history with it. The Scotsman, for its part, reports that a novel has been named Scottish Book of the Year, calling it a masterpiece by one of the finest Scottish novelists writing today. The Scotsman piece as I have it doesn't name the author, so I can't confirm that it is the same win, though it seems very likely. Either way, it is a pleasure to see a novelist celebrated for what he does best, which is drawing characters you can't stop thinking about in a Glasgow you can step straight into, without needing to know it first. If you have ever thought of putting Shuggie Bain in front of older students, this is a good moment to mention it.

There is also a charming piece from Upworthy about Stevie Nicks. She reportedly misheard a Southern woman's accent, and that one vowel became the seed of one of her best-known songs. The piece is short and I won't name the song, but I like the story, because it shows how a misheard word can turn into art. It is a lovely little lesson about sound, dialect and the way language gives writers things they never planned. It would make a rather good starter for a lesson on accent and voice.

Last, a note rather than good news. Upworthy also carries a reflective piece by a parent who showed Dead Poets Society to their Gen Z children and was floored by how angry the children were with it. It isn't really uplifting, but as someone who teaches literature, you may find it interesting to read how a film about a teacher lands with young people today, and perhaps compare it with how your own students respond.

That is all for this morning, Yamuna, and I hope something here makes it into your day, whether it is a curlew, a painting, or a thirty-minute walk through Trastevere.

He calls it playful, ironic and very limited. It's the sort of question that will no doubt find its way into a classroom discussion before long.

If you'd like something to watch this week, ARTE has two documentaries on Rome. The first, "Vatican, la cité qui voulait devenir éternelle", is available until the twenty-seventh of January. It follows how Saint Peter's tomb became the centre of the Catholic Church and a great political and artistic hub, drawing on the Vatican's archives, manuscripts, architecture and painting. The second, "Saint-Pierre de Rome", looks at the biggest building site of the Renaissance, using archives from the years fifteen-oh-six to sixteen twenty-six. The timing is good, because the basilica marks its four-hundredth anniversary on the eighteenth of November. And for the classical music lover in you, the BBC has announced a new series called "Beethoven: Rise of a Genius", to mark two hundred years since the composer's death. There's no broadcast date or platform yet, but it's one to watch for.

A word for your BFI corner. Theatre and Tonic has published a review of Great Expectations at the Jack Studio Theatre. With Dickens on the twenty-twenty-seven programme, it could be a useful way to think about Pip, and about the novel's life on stage. There's also a short essay from MiscelAna, marking four hundred and ten years since Shakespeare's death and asking why he still matters. It's brief, but it could work as an opening for seconde or première, whether you're heading into Twelfth Night or Hamlet.

On the education front, a quick note from franceinfo. The Education minister, Edouard Geffray, has told Le Parisien that he won't change the baccalauréat calendar, despite the hours lost in lycées that have been blockaded. He also says he wants more transparency around Parcoursup. Of course, you'll know better than most how that lands in a staff room.

And to finish with some good news. Karl Bushby, a British former paratrooper, has completed a walk around the world that began in Hull in nineteen ninety-eight. He's now back in his hometown on foot, and, according to Good News Network, reunited with his tearful mother after twenty-eight years. It's a story with a proper arc: a departure, a long road, and a homecoming. There's a gentler tale from Upworthy, too. An artist had been evicted after forty years, so that her landlord's family could claim her hand-painted murals. A neighbour with a paint sprayer stepped in with a parting gift, and by all accounts it was perfect. It's a small story about kindness, art and what a place means to the people who've made it beautiful.

That's your Sunday, Yamuna. I hope the day brings you good colour, good company and a good book.
